title: Adaptive, reward-based phishing training aimed at the riskiest employees first
problem: A small group of repeat clickers is said to cause most phishing incidents, and blanket annual training treats everyone the same.
approach: Qualcomm enrolled its 1,000 highest-risk employees in Hoxhunt's adaptive programme, benchmarked them against colleagues, and won support for rollout to about 48,000.
Avanade ran a three-month trial of two 1,000-user groups; Hoxhunt showed a 43% higher resilience ratio and 11% lower failure rate (vendor-published).
Qualcomm says company-wide failure rates fell by a factor of 6 (vendor-published). The security team selects the cohort and decides the rollout.

title: Behaviour-signal-driven human risk management with just-in-time micro-training and nudges
problem: Uber judged compliance-based awareness training could not reduce risk effectively, and wanted a programme for over 25,000 users with a two-person team.
approach: Uber and Hoxhunt's programme uses behavioural signals to trigger micro-learning at moments of risk, with content chosen 'with AI capabilities'.
Training completion rose from 60% to over 90% and simulated threat reporting tripled (vendor-published).
The security team defines escalation playbooks and intervention triggers. Research prototypes TrainShield and CyberGLA go further, with no outcome figures.

title: AI-generated and AI-agent-built security awareness content and campaigns
problem: Training content libraries have gaps for organisation-specific policies, new attacks and incidents; building modules takes days and waiting on a vendor takes longer.
approach: Hoxhunt's Content Studio turns a prompt and the customer's documents into a draft module; the vendor claims minutes instead of days, unmeasured.
A person reviews and publishes every generated module. KnowBe4 said in January 2026 it has seven AI agents in market (vendor-published).
Two controlled studies (N=480) found learning gains from AI-generated training but no advantage from complex personalisation (independent).

title: Personalised, public-information-driven spear-phishing simulations inside awareness programmes
problem: Generic simulations may under-represent what attackers can now do cheaply; spear phishing is about 0.1% of phishing emails but linked to 66% of breaches in one cited study.
approach: At TU Braunschweig, 7,700 participants got AI-written emails tailored from web searches; click rate was 10.0% versus 3.7% and 4.1% generic (independent).
Personalisation cost about USD 0.03 per email (independent).
Ethics and staff-committee review precede launch, and participants are briefed and debriefed. Adaptive Security lists a similar product.
who: TU Braunschweig, Adaptive Security, academic researchers

title: Conversational voice and text-message phishing practice with AI-voice scenarios
problem: Employees are trained to scrutinise emails, but a live call demands instant reaction; in a survey experiment, 16.5% said they would or might comply with AI voice scams.
approach: Hoxhunt describes training where employees practise against an AI voice in simulated phone conversations that adapt to their responses.
Adaptive lists voice-call and SMS phishing simulations; no customer names or results published (vendor-published).
The awareness team reviews scenario design and results.

title: Deepfake and executive-impersonation drills for finance, help desk and executive staff
problem: Arup confirmed a Hong Kong employee paid out about USD 25 million after a video call with deepfake colleagues.
approach: NYDFS tells regulated entities training can use simulated phishing and voice and video impersonation exercises, covering verification of unexpected money-transfer requests.
Vendors including KnowBe4 and Adaptive sell deepfake simulations; none reported outcomes, and no tested reduction in fraud was found.
Human review and oversight sit inside the verification procedures for money transfers.

title: Automated triage of employee-reported suspicious emails
problem: Once training works, employees report more suspicious emails; Avanade's people 'began reporting far more threats', a volume hard to analyse manually.
approach: Avanade used Hoxhunt's platform to categorise and prioritise reported messages automatically, reporting over 900 hours a month of analyst time saved (vendor-published).
It reports a 98% reduction in false positives and incident escalations (vendor-published).
Microsoft documents a Defender Phishing Triage Agent that classifies reports with a written rationale; analysts review it and can give feedback.

title: Behavioural-AI email security replacing the email gateway and answering employee reports
problem: Valvoline still saw spear phishing and invoice fraud reach inboxes despite a secure email gateway, native security and awareness training.
approach: Valvoline moved to Abnormal's API-based behavioural AI, removed its gateway, and gave users personalised replies to their reports.
Valvoline cites USD 600K in loss avoided from stopping one recurring invoice fraud, and 480 analyst hours saved monthly (vendor-published).
Analysts still handle reports and dashboards, and the security team uses the dashboard to spot attack trends.

title: Idea: AI as second reader of inbound email intent to warn users
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: AI-written, personalised lures remove the language errors users were trained to spot.
approach: A research study found Claude 3.5 Sonnet detected email intent with accuracy well above 90% and low false positives (independent).
It also flagged some seemingly benign messages that passed human detection.
A warning is shown to the user, who decides.

title: AI-driven detection and automated takedown of brand and executive impersonation
problem: ARK Invest faced impersonation across LinkedIn, Instagram, WhatsApp and Telegram; removing scams took 'days to weeks', and it received hundreds of concerned calls and emails yearly.
approach: ARK adopted Doppel's platform, which detects impersonation across domains, social media and the dark web, and acts on takedowns, not just flags.
Doppel reports a 5.5-hour median domain resolution time and 98% takedown success (vendor-published).
ARK says reported impersonations roughly halved from about 400 in 2024 to 2025 (self-reported). Human checkpoints are not described.

title: AI scam-baiting honeypots to extract mule accounts and map scam workflows
problem: Detection, training and takedown do not remove the infrastructure scammers rely on, such as mule bank accounts; long-running trust scams are hard to study.
approach: A research system used AI to hold weeks-long conversations with scammers, starting more than 2,600 engagements over five months.
Its information disclosure rate, for items such as mule accounts, was about 32% (independent).
Human operators compared against the AI's replies in evaluation; acceptance was about 70% (independent).
who: Academic researchers; BSides Las Vegas talk

title: Identity and liveness checks on remote hires (fake IT worker defence)
problem: The FBI says North Korean IT workers have used AI and face-swapping in video job interviews; KnowBe4 hired one who passed four interviews and background checks.
approach: KnowBe4 detected the hire when endpoint detection flagged malware on the shipped laptop; its security team called the new hire.
The FBI advises identity verification through interviewing, onboarding and employment, cross-checking HR records, and educating HR staff.
Datadog describes a detection stack that includes AI-driven risk assessment. No AI effectiveness figures published.

title: Idea: out-of-band, deepfake-aware verification for payment and credential requests
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: video, voice and email can all be synthesised, and regulators report more suspicious-activity filings describing suspected deepfake media.
approach: Regulator-recommended approach: treat any voice or video request for money, credentials or data as unverified until confirmed through a separate channel.
NYDFS says training should cover verifying unexpected transfer requests and when human review must be part of verification.
No outcome figures published.

title: AI-based insider-threat log analysis
problem: Dedicated staff cannot manually examine the volume of logs needed to catch insider threats.
approach: RedChronos, the authors' system at Xiaohongshu, analyses logs with an AI model using weighted voting and a genetic algorithm.
It reduced log samples engineers must analyse by approximately 90% (self-reported).
Engineers still analyse flagged samples; it assists, not replaces. A separate 2026 framework gained 11.40 F1 points on a public dataset (independent).

title: Insider-risk programmes with AI-assisted detection, risk scoring and investigation
problem: Negligent or mistaken insiders are the largest driver of insider-risk cost, and incidents take on average 67 days to contain.
approach: Microsoft documents Purview Insider Risk Management, which correlates signals into policies, alerts and cases, pseudonymises users by default and keeps audit logs.
Above Security was reported at Black Hat USA 2026 offering AI-native insider-risk investigations. In a Ponemon/DTEX survey, 42% use AI (vendor-published).
Risk analysts act on cases and escalate to eDiscovery where needed.

title: Shadow-AI visibility and point-of-risk coaching: 'audit and educate' instead of block
problem: Employees put internal documents, source code and meeting content into public AI tools, and AI browsers and agents can bypass traditional logging.
approach: DTEX's CTO describes shifting from block-first to audit and educate, with prompt inspection and real-time nudges.
Adaptive lists an AI Governance product; KnowBe4 announced an Agent Risk Manager browser extension, in early access for some US customers.
DTEX's CTO claims containment time fell 17%, from 81 to 67 days (vendor-published). Human checkpoints are not described.

title: Idea: AI voice agents in authorised phone-scam red-team tests of help desks
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: help desks and finance staff handle voice requests attackers can now automate, and human-caller testing is slow and limited.
approach: Practitioner activity only: DEF CON 34 lists a 'Battle of the Bots: Vishing Edition' contest; ScamBench appears at BSides Las Vegas 2026.
No results for the contest were found.
A red-team lead approves scenarios.

title: Idea: sequence analysis of real social-engineering calls to design detection and training
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: social engineering is usually described as isolated techniques, while real interactions follow sequences.
approach: A BSides Las Vegas conference talk describes analysing over 1,200 call transcripts to see whether interaction steps follow stable ordering patterns.
The aim is to inform detection, red teaming and training. No results published beyond the talk abstract.
Human checkpoints are not described.
